sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Iūppiter** (*iuppiter*) — The Father of the Sky — belongs to the Roman tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Sky, Thunder, Sovereignty". The name means "'Sky-father' (from *Dyēu-pater)"[^1].

Iūppiter is the god in whose name Rome swore: Optimus Maximus, "best and greatest," the witness of every treaty, the dedicatee of every victory, and the direct linguistic heir of the Indo-European sky father — the oldest divine name the West still speaks.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Iūppiter** and serves its temple at [iūppiter.com](https://xn--ippiter-0sb.com). The restoration preserves the long vowel ū — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses — which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *iuppiter* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.
Varro, De Lingua Latina / Antiquitates Rerum Divinarum, Loeb Classical Library, 45 BCE.
Cicero, Marcus Tullius — collected works, Loeb Classical Library, 43 BCE.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Iūppiter** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "'Sky-father' (from *Dyēu-pater)"[^1].

The ASCII form *iuppiter* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Iūppiter** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves the long vowel ū — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses — which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **i** → **I** — Same letter
- **u** → **ū** — Macron marks the long vowel
- **p** → **p** — Same letter
- **p** → **p** — Same letter
- **i** → **i** — Same letter
- **t** → **t** — Same letter
- **e** → **e** — Same letter
- **r** → **r** — Same letter

The project holds the domain **iūppiter.com** (xn--ippiter-0sb.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Ennius, Annales, ed. Skutsch, The Annals of Q. Ennius (1985), 180 BCE.
Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro), Aeneid / Eclogues / Georgics, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 19 BCE.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈjuːp.pi.ter/** — Classical Latin.[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: YOO-pi-ter, with the geminate pp and long ū.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Latin** — Iūppiter
- **Greek twin** — Ζεύς
- **Vedic twin** — Dyaus-pitā
- **Owned form** — Iūppiter

Iūppiter compounds the vocative of the sky-father's ancient name — Dyēu-pəter, "O Father Sky" — the same formula that gives Greek Zeús and Vedic Dyaus-pitā. The doubled pp is the standard classical spelling; both macrons are certain, and the name is Latin's oldest continuous theonym.

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.body:
The original script for this roman name has not yet been added to PUNICODEX. The form shown is a scholarly transliteration.[^1]

The form **Iūppiter** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Iūppiter is the god in whose name Rome swore: Optimus Maximus, "best and greatest," the witness of every treaty, the dedicatee of every victory, and the direct linguistic heir of the Indo-European sky father — the oldest divine name the West still speaks.[^1]

### The Thunderbolt

His weapon and signature — the bolt that marks where sovereignty lands.

### The Capitol

His great temple, dedicated in 509 BCE — the year of the Republic's own beginning.

### The Eagle

The bird at the head of every legion; to lose its standard was Rome's deepest shame.

### The Triumph

The general robed as the god for one day — and the slave whispering mortality in his ear.

sources.citation: Varro, De Lingua Latina / Antiquitates Rerum Divinarum, Loeb Classical Library, 45 BCE.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Iūppiter concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The thunderbolt** — The sky's verdict; sovereignty as sudden light
- **The eagle** — The highest flier, the king of birds for the king of gods
- **The oak** — The tree of Dodona and of the civic crown — strength that shelters
- **The flint** — Iuppiter Lapis, the stone by which oaths were sworn

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Roman myth made Zeús' biography his own, but Iūppiter's truest stories are Roman institutions: the oath, the triumph, the dedication of spoils — religion as constitutional machinery.[^1]

### Iovem Lapidem (The Oath)

The most binding Roman oath was sworn per Iovem Lapidem — by Jupiter the Stone — while holding a flint from his altar and reciting the formula of the fetial priests: "If I deceive, may Iuppiter strike me as I strike this pig." Law, treaty, and contract all rested on his witness; the stone was his body in the courtroom of nations.[^2]

### The Borrowed Face (The Triumph)

In the triumph, the victorious general rode in Iūppiter's own regalia — purple and gold, face painted red like the god's terracotta statue — while a slave held the crown and whispered "memento mori." Rome let its greatest man borrow the god's face for one day, and made the god remind him to give it back: sovereignty rehearsed and returned.

### Opima Spolia (The Spoils)

The rarest honour in Rome belonged to Iūppiter Feretrius: the spolia opima, "rich spoils," taken when a Roman commander slew the enemy king in single combat — won by Romulus, by Cossus, and by Marcellus at Clastidium (222 BCE), and never again. Augustus blocked the fourth claimant on a technicality: some honours were too royal for an emperor's subjects.

### The Standard (The Eagle)

Every legion carried his aquila into battle, and its loss was the deepest disgrace Rome knew — the eagles of Varus' three legions, lost in the Teutoburg Forest, were recovered a generation later by Germanicus' campaigns and treated as returning citizens. The sky father marched, in bronze, at the head of the army that built the Mediterranean's order.

sources.citation: Varro, De Lingua Latina / Antiquitates Rerum Divinarum, Loeb Classical Library, 45 BCE.
Cicero, Marcus Tullius — collected works, Loeb Classical Library, 43 BCE.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Everywhere Rome went, Iūppiter wore local faces: Zeús in the East, Ammon in Egypt (Alexander's "father"), Dolichenus in the Syrian legionary cult — a storm god in iron scale-armour worshipped by soldiers from Britain to the Danube — and the Celtic wheel-god Taranis on Jupiter-columns of the Rhineland. His very name is the syncretism that precedes all others: Zeús, Dyaus, Tiwaz, and Iūppiter are one father spoken in four dialects.[^1]

Within the Roman tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[diana|Diāna]], [[ianus|Iānus]], [[iuno|Iūnō]], [[neptunus|Neptūnus]], [[vulcanus|Vulcānus]], and [[anu|Anû]].

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: "By Jove" keeps the oath in English; "jovial" preserves his planetary temperament; Thursday (dies Iovis, jeudi, giovedì) is his weekday across Romance Europe. Astronomy gave him the largest planet — fittingly, since Galileo's discovery of Jupiter's moons cracked the geocentric cosmos. Every invocation of supreme authority in the Western tradition is, etymologically, still addressed to the father sky.[^1]

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: The Capitoline temple of Iuppiter Optimus Maximus — dedicated 509 BCE, burned and rebuilt repeatedly — is documented by its massive podium under the Palazzo Caffarelli and by Pliny's and Dionysius' descriptions of its triple cella. The Jupiter-columns of the German provinces (reconstructed at Mainz, Stuttgart, and Hausen) show him riding down the giants. His oak of Dodona belongs to his Greek brother, but the flint-knives of the fetial oath and the aquilae standards of the legions fill the museums of two continents.[^1]

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.label: Epithets & Epicleses
sections.body:
Rome's god accumulated titles the way the city accumulated provinces.

- **Optimus Maximus** — 'Best and Greatest'; the Capitoline title, the state's formal address to him.
- **Feretrius** — 'of the Spoils'; the small, ancient Capitoline shrine of the spolia opima.
- **Capitolinus** — 'of the Capitol'; his civic residence-title.
- **Stator** — 'the Stayer'; Romulus' vow-title, the god who stops the rout.
- **Tonans** — 'the Thunderer'; Augustus' title after his narrow escape from lightning.
- **Lapis** — 'of the Stone'; the flint-oath, his most legal aspect.
- **Invictus** — 'the Unconquered'; the late-antique warrior-title.

sources.citation: Livy 1.12 (Stator), 10.28–29; Suetonius, Augustus 29 (Tonans).

sections.label: Oracle & Cult Sites
sections.body: The **Capitoline temple** — Iuppiter Optimus Maximus Capitolinus — was Rome's religious centre of gravity: vowed by the last kings, dedicated in 509 BCE as the Republic's first act, rebuilt after the fires of 83 BCE and 69 CE, its gilded doors and triple cella described by a dozen ancient authors. The small shrine of **Iuppiter Feretrius** beside it was said to be the city's first temple of all, founded by Romulus for the spoils of kings. In the provinces, his **Jupiter-columns** of the Rhineland and the legionary shrines of Dolichenus from Britain to Syria map the god's imperial diaspora in stone.

sources.citation: Dionysius 4.61; the Capitoline excavation reports (Pietrangeli).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Iūppiter is the god of the spoken bond. Lightning, empire, and law are one idea in his name: that the highest power is the one by which promises are kept. Every signature, every oath of office, every treaty since has borrowed his architecture — the sky as witness, the word as bond, the bolt as the penalty for perjury of the soul.

And the oaths continue, translated but recognizable: every courtroom's "the whole truth," every inauguration's raised hand, every treaty signed before witnesses rehearses the per Iovem Lapidem — the appeal to a witness greater than the parties. The Romans' insight stands unimproved: promises between mortals need a sky to be sworn by, or they are only weather.[^1]

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.
